summary: Changes the schedule for moving from the old Telnet to the new one, after worries about a coordinated switch. New Telnet implementations were still to be ready on 1 January 1974 but were to use ICP socket 23.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 593 changes how the network would introduce new Telnet and FTP implementations. It assigns new Telnet to socket 23 for testing and keeps FTP on socket 21 until a later changeover decision.

questions: why did rfc 593 change the telnet schedule
which socket did new telnet use
subtitle: A revised schedule for implementing new Telnet and FTP versions.

tldr.problem: Implementers and users were concerned about coordinating the change from old to new Telnet because the versions could be incompatible.
tldr.mechanism: New Telnet servers and clients were to use ICP socket 23 while the network assessed readiness; new FTP implementations would keep using socket 21 until a change was judged appropriate.
tldr.outcome: The RFC retains the planned readiness dates but defers a network-wide changeover until it can happen without disrupting user services.

today: RFC 593 records a 1973 schedule change for introducing new Telnet and FTP implementations.

sections.title: A Coordinated Telnet Changeover
sections.content: Several Telnet implementers and users raised concerns about coordinating the move from the old protocol to the new one, including possible incompatibilities described in RFC 559. The authors revised the changeover plan to give implementations a way to be tested without interfering with normal service.
sections.plainLanguage: Users and implementers worried that switching Telnet versions together could disrupt service. The RFC changes the plan to provide a separate place for new implementations.

sections.title: New Telnet on ICP Socket 23
sections.content:
New Telnet implementations were still to be ready by January 1, 1974, but servers were to listen on ICP socket 23 and user programs were to connect there. The RFC says it would be useful for clients to let users select the server socket and for servers to handle both protocols, as MIT-DMCG had done, so implementers could test and debug the new version.

During January, technical liaisons would be surveyed. They would be notified when implementations were ready for a changeover that would not disrupt user services.
sections.plainLanguage: The new Telnet was assigned socket 23 while sites tested it. Network liaisons would assess readiness before announcing a change that could affect users.

sections.title: FTP Remains on ICP Socket 21
sections.content: The RFC also changes the FTP schedule in light of the Telnet plan. New FTP implementations were still to be ready by February 1, 1974, but were to continue using ICP socket 21 until the network could determine that changing it was appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: New FTP implementations could be prepared, but they would continue to use socket 21 until the network decided a changeover was suitable.
